While DAP’s Ngeh Koo Ham (Harapan-Beruas) questioned the use of the term “bumiputera” in official statistics, PAS' Nik Zawawi Salleh (PN-Pasir Puteh) urged the government to strengthen national unity and better manage racial differences. Ngeh urged the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) to use the term “Malay” instead of “bumiputera”, claiming that the latter category also includes Muslim foreigners. Meanwhile, Zawawi cautioned against constantly finding fault with others, warning that such attitudes could deepen divisions within Malaysia’s multiracial society. “If we keep looking for faults in others, bringing up this and that, we will eventually end up fighting among ourselves. “Allah created us in Malaysia as a multiracial society. We have people of different races and ethnic backgrounds,” he said. Zawawi stressed that Malaysians, regardless of race or ethnicity, shared a common humanity. “Whether we are talking about the Orang Asli, Malays, Chinese, or Indians... even Jelutong and I are family,” he said, referring to RSN Rayer (Harapan-Jelutong). He also called for greater emphasis on national unity initiatives under Budget 2027, including establishing a special committee chaired by either the prime minister or deputy prime minister. “The agenda of fostering unity among the various communities in our country is something that only a government can effectively implement. “Therefore, I hope this year’s budget will include measures towards achieving this objective,” he said. Zawawi made the remarks during his own debate on the Supply Bill 2027, without directly referring to Ngeh’s statements. Definition dispute Earlier, Ngeh expressed surprise over what he claimed was DOSM’s use of the term bumiputera to include Muslim foreigners residing in Malaysia. He compared the ethnic composition of voters in the Beruas parliamentary constituency in 2022, comprising 56.8 percent Chinese, 27.2 percent Malays, 15.2 percent Indians, and approximately 0.9 percent others, with population figures for 2023 published in DOSM’s 2025 report. He said the report, which provided the closest available data for comparison, showed that the constituency’s population comprised 47.6 percent Chinese, 34.8 percent bumiputera, 17.1 percent Indians, and 0.5 percent others. The report also recorded that non-citizens accounted for 7.5 percent of the population in Beruas. “This means Rohingya, Bangladeshi, Indonesian, Pakistani, and other Muslims in Malaysia are classified as bumiputera,” he claimed. According to Ngeh, the term "bumiputera" does not appear in any Malaysian law, while existing legal provisions only provide for affirmative action benefiting Malays, the indigenous peoples of Sabah and Sarawak, and the Orang Asli. “If the term is used, it should be restricted to these three groups of Malaysian citizens. “Otherwise, assistance will be channelled to groups that are not the intended beneficiaries under the law, creating a situation where outsiders are favoured while our own people are neglected,” he said. Ngeh also cited Article 160(2) of the Federal Constitution, which he said sets out four criteria for defining a Malay: professing Islam, habitually speaking Malay, conforming to Malay customs, and being born in Malaya before 1957 or descended from such individuals. He argued that Muslims who arrived in the country after 1957 could not be defined as Malays or be entitled to government privileges intended for Malays. “If this definition is not corrected, our nation’s wealth and resources will be used to enrich foreigners at the expense of Malays, the indigenous peoples of Sabah and Sarawak, and our Orang Asli. “The issue of bumiputera poverty will never be resolved if foreigners are included, as many of them come from impoverished backgrounds. “Foreigners who have become Malaysian citizens can be treated fairly and equally, but they should not be placed in a category that gives them priority over existing citizens,” said Ngeh. Beyond the criteria Ngeh listed, Article 160(2) also covers descendants of those who meet its historical conditions, including provisions relating to birth or domicile in the Federation or Singapore before independence. PARLIAMENT | Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo said civil servants can use other navigation apps and are not restricted to the locally developed TuJu app, after the government banned Waze for official duties. Speaking during Minister's Question Time, Gobind (above) stressed that the restriction applied specifically to Waze and did not require civil servants to switch exclusively to TuJu. "There is no statement saying that we can only use TuJu. We can still use other applications, such as Google Maps," he said in response to a supplementary question from Young Syefura Othman (Harapan-Bentong). Gobind also clarified that the ban, announced by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim yesterday, applied only to civil servants carrying out official duties and not to the general public. "Firstly, the ban applies to government employees or civil servants, as defined under the Federal Constitution. It does not apply to all Malaysians. "Secondly, it only applies to official matters," he said. The minister said the restriction stemmed from concerns about data security and legal jurisdiction, particularly because Waze’s terms of service are subject to Israeli law. "Based on the information I have received, even if we do not use Waze, our movements can still be determined through the application. "When we examine the agreement, it is clear that it falls under the jurisdiction of Israeli law. That becomes a problem for us," he said. Gobind argued that Malaysians could face difficulties seeking legal recourse in Israel if disputes arose over the application. "That is why we have imposed the ban on Waze, specifically because of legal and security considerations," he said. He also pointed out that, under its terms of service, the application handled data collected through it in Israel. TuJu still being improved Earlier, Young Syefura questioned whether TuJu was ready to replace Waze, citing complaints about its performance. She said she had downloaded and tested the application herself but found it disappointing. "I downloaded the TuJu application myself, but it was actually rather disappointing. "We have also seen responses from the public saying that the application is not yet sufficiently developed for use at this stage," she said. Works Minister Alexander Nanta Linggi launched TuJu in November last year, and it was developed through a collaboration between the Malaysian Highway Authority and Prosignal Consortium Sdn Bhd. Gobind, who acknowledged the criticism, explained that TuJu was originally developed for highway navigation rather than comprehensive road coverage. He said the application was designed to provide information on highway traffic conditions, toll plazas, rest and service areas, and closed-circuit television footage showing congestion. However, efforts were ongoing to expand its coverage beyond highways, including traffic conditions on roads leading to major expressways. "I agree with what Bentong has raised.
